what.text: Tribulus terrestris (puncture vine) is a plant used in herbal medicine for sexual function and fertility. Its effects are attributed to steroidal saponins, mainly protodioscin.

what.text: In the US it is sold as a botanical dietary supplement, often promoted for strength and muscle. FDA does not review supplements before sale.

what.text: Tribulus is not an approved drug. Trials on testosterone mostly found no change.

research.text: Randomized trials of tribulus in men are small to medium in size. Several found no change in testosterone. A 2026 meta-analysis of 8 trials found higher erectile function scores than placebo but no difference in total testosterone.

research.title: Androgens in healthy young men (Neychev and Mitev)

facts.v: randomized, placebo-controlled trial, two dose groups
21 healthy men aged 20 to 36
4 weeks
testosterone, androstenedione and LH at six time points

research.found: No difference from placebo in testosterone, androstenedione or LH.

src.label: Neychev and Mitev, J Ethnopharmacol, 2005

research.title: Elite rugby league players in preseason (Rogerson et al.)

facts.v: match-paired, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
22 elite male rugby league players, average age 20
450 mg tribulus extract a day or placebo, with training
5 weeks
strength, fat-free mass, urinary testosterone/epitestosterone (T/E) ratio

research.found: Strength and fat-free mass rose in both groups, with no difference between them. The T/E ratio did not change.

src.label: Rogerson et al., J Strength Cond Res, 2007

research.title: Erectile dysfunction, 30 men (Santos et al.)

facts.v: prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled
30 men aged 40 and over with erectile dysfunction
800 mg tribulus a day or placebo
30 days
erectile function (IIEF-5) and total testosterone

research.found: Scores rose over time in both groups, with no difference between tribulus and placebo. Testosterone did not differ.

src.label: Santos et al., Actas Urol Esp, 2014

research.title: Male sexual dysfunction, 180 men (Kamenov et al.)

facts.v: prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (described as Phase IV)
180 men aged 18 to 65 with mild or moderate erectile dysfunction, with or without low sexual desire; 86 per group completed
a standardized Bulgarian tribulus extract tablet (250 mg) or placebo, 3 × 2 tablets a day
12 weeks
change in erectile function (IIEF) score; blood lipids; safety

research.found: IIEF scores improved more on tribulus than on placebo.

src.label: Kamenov et al., Maturitas, 2017

research.title: Aging men with low testosterone, ED and urinary symptoms (GamalEl Din et al.)

facts.v: randomized, placebo-controlled trial
70 aging men with partial androgen deficiency, erectile dysfunction and lower urinary tract symptoms
3 months
total testosterone, erectile function (Arabic IIEF-5), prostate symptom score, PSA, liver enzymes

research.found: In the tribulus group, total testosterone and erectile function scores rose from baseline. Urinary symptoms did not worsen. PSA and the liver enzyme AST rose slightly.

src.label: GamalEl Din et al., Urologia, 2019

research.title: Tribulus for erectile dysfunction: 8 trials (Suharyani et al.)

facts.v: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials
erectile function (IIEF-5, IIEF-15), total testosterone, adverse events

research.found: Erectile function scores were higher with tribulus than with placebo (IIEF-5 mean difference 3.23). Total testosterone did not differ. Adverse event rates did not differ.

us.text: Tribulus terrestris is sold in the US as a dietary supplement. It is not an FDA-approved drug, and FDA does not review supplements for safety or effectiveness before sale. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: Tribulus terrestris is a botanical. Under US law, a product meant to supplement the diet that contains an herb or other botanical can be sold as a dietary supplement.

src.label: 21 U.S.C. 321(ff), definition of dietary supplement, govinfo

items.text: FDA does not have the authority to approve dietary supplements before they are marketed, and a firm generally does not have to give FDA its safety evidence. FDA does not approve supplements or their labelling.

after.text: Tribulus terrestris is not named on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List or the 2027 list. In a 5-week trial in rugby players, it did not change the urinary T/E ratio used in doping tests.

side.text: Trials report few side effects, and a meta-analysis found adverse event rates similar to placebo. Case reports describe serious kidney and liver injury and breast growth in men who used tribulus.

items.text: adverse events were similar to placebo across 8 trials. In one 3-month trial, the liver enzyme AST and PSA rose slightly.

items.lead: Kidney and liver injury, case reports:
items.text: a young man developed liver, kidney and nerve toxicity, with a seizure, after drinking tribulus water for 2 days. A 46-year-old man developed severe jaundice and kidney injury after 2 months of tribulus supplements and recovered after plasmapheresis.
